texts.label: text
texts.orig: When my great-aunt Florence died, she left me something nobody in the family had expected: a small, white lighthouse on a rocky island off the west coast. I had visited her there only once, as a child, and I remembered three things about the place. The wind never stopped, the stairs were impossibly steep, and the kitchen always smelt of fresh bread and paraffin.
texts.text: When my great-aunt Florence died, she left me something nobody in the family had expected: a small, white lighthouse on a rocky island off the west coast. I had visited her there only once, as a child, and I remembered three things about the place. The wind never stopped, the stairs were impossibly steep, and the kitchen always smelt of fresh bread and paraffin.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The solicitor's office was on the first floor of an old building near the harbour. Mr Fielding, a thin man with enormous eyebrows, read the will aloud and then pushed a brown envelope across the desk. "Your aunt was very specific," he said. "The lighthouse is yours, but only if you spend fifty nights there before the end of the year."

Mr Fielding, a thin man with enormous eyebrows, read the will aloud and then pushed a brown envelope across the desk. "Your aunt was very specific," he said. "The lighthouse is yours, but only if you spend fifty nights there before the end of the year."

texts.label: text
texts.orig: "Fifty nights?" I repeated. "Alone?" He nodded, as if this were a perfectly reasonable request, and added that the official paperwork would take several weeks. I signed everything, shook his hand and walked out into the rain, wondering whether I had just made the most adventurous decision of my life or the most irresponsible one.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The ferry left me on the island at four o'clock on a grey October afternoon. The captain, a cheerful woman called Fiona, promised to come back every Friday with supplies. "If the weather is bad, I'll be late," she warned. "If it's really bad, I won't come at all." Then she waved, turned the boat around and disappeared into the mist.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Inside, the lighthouse was colder than I had imagined. I lit the old stove, found a fluffy blanket in a cupboard and made myself a cup of tea. On the kitchen table there was a leather notebook with my name written on the cover in Florence's careful, old-fashioned handwriting. The first page contained a single sentence: 'Read one entry every evening, and not a page more.'

On the kitchen table there was a leather notebook with my name written on the cover in Florence's careful, old-fashioned handwriting. The first page contained a single sentence: 'Read one entry every evening, and not a page more.'

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Naturally, I wanted to read the whole thing immediately. Nevertheless, something about the instruction made me hesitate. My aunt had been a remarkably efficient woman who never did anything without a reason, so I closed the notebook, finished my tea and climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The entries turned out to be a mixture of practical advice and strange, affectionate observations. One evening she explained how to fix the generator when the flame in the pilot light went out. Another evening she described a family of seals that, according to her, had been arguing about the same flat rock for twenty years.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Gradually, I began to understand the rhythm of the island. I learned to read the sky, to recognise the difference between a temporary shower and a serious storm, and to appreciate the extraordinary silence that followed the wind. I stopped checking my phone, which rarely had a signal anyway, and started writing my own reflections in the margins of Florence's notebook.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: On the thirty-first night, the entry was different. 'By now,' she had written, 'you have probably noticed that the third step from the top is loose. Lift it carefully.' I took a torch, climbed the stairs and, with considerable difficulty, lifted the step. Underneath there was a flat tin box containing a bundle of letters, a photograph of a young woman on a fishing boat and a key.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I won't tell you everything I discovered during the remaining nineteen nights, because some of it belongs to Florence and some of it now belongs to me. I will only say that the key opened a drawer in the office of the harbour master, and that the letters told the story of a friendship which had lasted, in secret, for more than sixty years.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When Fiona collected me on the fiftieth morning, she looked at my face and laughed. "You're not leaving, are you?" she asked. She was right. I went back to the mainland to sign the final documents, and two weeks later I returned to the island with a suitcase, a box of books and a new notebook of my own.
